coach_says: Your knight on f6 is pinned to your queen by Bg5, and Nd5 is already attacking it, so its only real defender is the knight on d7. White's threat was Bb5, hitting that defender, and b6 does nothing about it: after Bb5 you lose material. When a piece is pinned and attacked twice, deal with that first, for example a6 to stop Bb5, or Kh8 to get out of the line.

The knight on c6 was the piece guarding your e5 pawn, so Nd4 leaves e5 hanging and White takes it with Nxe5. Worse, that knight then joins the bishop on c4 in hitting f7, threatening Nxf7 forking your queen and rook. Before you move a piece, check what it was protecting; here d5 hits back in the centre instead.

White's knight on f3 is attacking your e5 pawn, and Bc5 doesn't defend it, so Nxe5 just wins a pawn. In the opening, always answer the question 'what does my opponent's last move threaten?' first. Nc6 develops a piece and protects e5 at the same time.

Three of your pieces were under attack here: the bishop on b5 by the c6 pawn, the knight on g5 by the h6 pawn, and the knight on e4 by Bf5. Qh5 saves none of them, and after hxg5 the h-file opens so the rook on h8 hits your queen too. When several pieces are attacked, count them and find a move that saves as many as possible, like Bd3, which retreats the bishop and guards e4.
also: queen on the same file as a rook

coach_says: Your bishop on d3 has almost no squares: e2 is taken by your queen, e4 and c2 by your pawns. Black was threatening c4, attacking it, and the only escape would be Bxc4 giving it up for a pawn. Re1 doesn't help, so after c4 you lose the bishop. Look for pawn moves that can trap a boxed-in piece; b3 stops c4 here.

Black's last move Ne6 attacked your bishop on f4, and nothing defends it. Bb3 goes after the d5 pawn but leaves the bishop hanging, so Nxf4 wins a whole piece. Before any plan, check whether your opponent's last move attacked something; Be5 or Bg3 keeps the bishop safe.

White was threatening Qf7, which is checkmate: the queen is protected by the rook on d7 and your king has no squares. Taking the h2 pawn ignores that, and Qf7# ends the game. When the opponent's queen and rook are near your king, look for their checks and mates first; Qg6 was the only move that covers f7.

You had two ways to block the check, and you blocked with the wrong piece. The rook on g7 was the key defender of your king, covering g7 and the seventh rank; moving it to g8 lets Qf6+ and Re7 bring mate. Bg8 blocks with the bishop instead and keeps the rook guarding, and then the game is about even. When blocking a check, ask what each blocking piece is defending now.
concept: blocked check with the wrong piece

coach_says: Your queen on d8 was the only defender of the knight on e7, which the rook on e4 attacks. Recapturing with the queen pulls it away, so Rxe7 just wins the knight. When you can recapture with more than one piece, check what each one is guarding; Nxc8 recaptures and keeps everything protected.
concept: recaptured with the knight's only defender

coach_says: White is already pushing the g-pawn towards your king, and g5 gives it something to bite on: h4 attacks g5 and opens the h-file towards your castled king. Pawn moves in front of your own king are hard to undo and make the opponent's attack easier. Here, start your own play on the queenside with b5 or Nb6 instead.
concept: gave the pawn storm a hook

coach_says: f6 opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, so after c3 kicks your knight White gets Bc4+ with check, and your knight has nowhere good to go (Nb3 loses to Bc4+ and Bxb3). Pawn moves next to your king can open lines you'll regret. Rfb8 was better, putting a rook on the open file and attacking the b5 pawn.
concept: opened a diagonal to your king

coach_says: Your king is stuck in the centre and Black's bishop on h6 controls the dark squares c1, d2 and g5. Nc3 removes the knight that was guarding d2, so Black's queen can come in via g5 or h4 towards d2, f2 and your king while your own queen is far away on e6. Here h4 takes g5 away from the black queen first; with an uncastled king, cover the entry squares before developing.

After g6, your dark-squared bishop is the piece that guards the holes on f6 and h6. Bh6 offers to trade it, and after Bxh6 Nxh6 Qd2 your knight is attacked on the rim and has to go back to g8, so you've lost time and your best defender. Fianchetto it with Bg7, or play d6 and develop.

f3 hits the queen, but White just takes the pawn with Nxf3 and develops a knight at the same time, so you've given away a pawn and helped White develop. Your f4 pawn was attacked, so the simple answer was to defend it while developing: Bh6 guards f4 and gets a piece out. Pushing a pawn to chase the queen is only good if the pawn can't simply be taken.
concept: pawn push that loses the pawn

coach_says: Your knight on f3 is pinned to your queen by the bishop on h5. gxf6 lets Black recapture with the queen on f6, adding a second attacker on that pinned knight, and Nd4 is coming too. When a piece is pinned, don't open lines for more attackers; Nbd2 adds a defender to f3 first.
concept: opened lines onto your pinned knight

coach_says: Black's knight on f6 is the only defender of the d5 pawn, so Bxf6 removes it and Nxd5 wins a second pawn, with the knight hitting the queen and c7. Retreating with Bg3 gives Black time for Qb4, attacking b2. When an enemy piece is guarding something, ask if you can take that guard off the board.

Black's b5 pawn was simply hanging to Bxb5, since your f1 bishop has a clear diagonal and nothing guards b5. Instead, a4 moves the pawn that was protecting b4, so Black plays Nxb4 and you only win your pawn back. Before pushing a pawn, check what it was protecting, and take free material when it's really free.
concept: missed a free pawn on b5

coach_says: d5 is about as good as anything here; you're already a couple of pawns down and the engine's choices are all close. Keep looking for activity for your pieces and chances against White's king rather than worrying about this move.

Qd3 is fine by the engine, so this isn't a mistake. In general though, you've now moved the queen three times in four moves; developing knights and bishops (Nf3, g3 and Bg2) is the habit that will serve you better.

You lose the queen whatever you do, because the knight check uncovered the bishop on h5. So the question is what you get back: Rxh2 takes the checking knight, and after Bxd1 you can win the bishop too with Bc6+ and Nxd1. Ke1 lets the knight escape to f3, so you end up a whole piece worse. When a knight gives check and you can capture it, look at taking it first.
